status_reason: Material, quantity (API concentration) and location (feed frame) are known, so a provisional assessment is possible; the old calibration cannot be approved for reuse and must be re-validated on the new blend.
answer: The old NIR calibration cannot be assumed valid for the new API and excipient blend, and adding Raman does not keep it valid either; both need a new model built and validated on the new blend. First test NIR on the new blend in the feed frame with laboratory-referenced samples, and compare against a combined NIR+Raman model fused on the same validation data.

inline.headline: Test NIR diffuse reflection on the new blend in the feed frame, with a new calibration built on laboratory-referenced samples
inline.install: Tablet press feed frame, probe inserted directly into the powder flow
inline.test_against: Raman fiber probe at 785 nm alone
inline.not_final_because: The old calibration is not valid for the new blend, so a new model is required; the silica fiber limit of 2400 nm is below the 2500 nm upper NIR limit and must be checked; no reference data for the new blend exist yet; the combined NIR+Raman model is only a hypothesis.

problems.text: The old calibration cannot be assumed valid for the new API and excipient blend. NIR models are built and validated for one matrix, so the new blend must be re-tested and most likely needs a new calibration.

Adding Raman does not keep the old calibration valid. Raman adds complementary information, and a combined NIR+Raman model is a new model fitted on fused data, so it needs its own calibration and validation; whether fusion helps this blend is still a hypothesis.
The silica Vis-NIR fiber transmits 350–2400 nm, while NIR is usually 780–2500 nm, so the top of the NIR range may be lost. Check the fiber and spectrometer range before testing.
Raman signals are weak and can be masked by fluorescence from organic compounds, so the new API and excipients must be checked for fluorescence before Raman is judged.

methods.why: Existing pilot method; detects hydrogen bonds and polar groups, diffuse reflection suits powders, and it works online with remote fiber probes.
Gives molecular backbone and non-polar group information complementary to NIR; a 785 nm Raman fiber probe was used in the feed-frame study, but signals are weak and fluorescence-prone.
Table 1 lists it for liquids, pastes and soft samples, and MIR is limited to layers below about 50 µm, so it does not fit a powder in the feed frame.
Useful only if the API or an excipient fluoresces; most chemicals do not.

experiment.objective: Test whether the current NIR calibration holds on the new blend, and whether a new NIR model or a fused NIR+Raman model predicts API concentration better.
steps: Prepare new-blend samples across the API range and obtain independent laboratory reference values for each.
Predict the new-blend samples with the old NIR calibration and record the error, to show the size of the matrix effect.
Record NIR diffuse-reflection and 785 nm Raman spectra of the same samples; check the fiber covers the measured range and look for fluorescence.
Build a new NIR model and a low-level fused NIR+Raman PLS model; validate both on held-out new-blend samples with segmented cross-validation and randomisation tests.
Compare the models on the same validation data; keep the fused model only if it beats NIR alone.
references: De Man, A, et al. (2024). Evaluating the improvement of blend potency measurements in the feed frame of a rotary tablet press using combined NIR and Raman spectroscopy. Analytical Chemistry, 96(26), 10586-10593.

multispectral.why: NIR detects hydrogen bonds and polar groups while Raman gives the molecular backbone and non-polar groups, so the information is complementary.
multispectral.test: Build NIR-only and fused NIR+Raman PLS models on the same new-blend validation samples; keep the fusion only if it predicts held-out API better than NIR alone.
